extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of humor, cognitive scientists, and theorists of laughter
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply John Morreall's account that humor consists in the enjoyment of a sudden cognitive shift; includes conditions that distinguish humor from other reactions and diagnostic questions for identifying humor. Useful for analyzing comedic examples and evaluating competing theories of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological shift occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychological shift occurs — from one mental state, expectation, or interpretation to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account requires there be an identifiable representation or interpretation in play before the comic moment and a different representation after; examples include a change of interpretation, reframing, or recognition of a pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift is sudden
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift is sudden (or at least quick enough to register as a switch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing matters: the change must be rapid enough to be experienced as a switch rather than a slow re-evaluation. Slow realizations may produce other responses (e.g., wonder) rather than immediate amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift is accompanied by pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift is accompanied by pleasure rather than by negative affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the change provokes fear, grief, anger, or disgust, it will not be experienced as humor. The hedonic tone at the moment of the shift must be positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is taken in the shift itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure is taken in the shift itself, not derived from the content of either state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is enjoyment of the cognitive move (the switch), not enjoyment of insulting, harmful, or otherwise content-based pleasures such as schadenfreude; examples include laughing at clever wordplay where no one is demeaned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive-shift types covered
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive-shift account subsumes various specific mechanisms: incongruity perception, resolution (puzzle → understanding), reframing, recognition (not seeing a pattern → seeing it), bisociation, and script switching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these labels as examples of the kinds of representational changes that can produce humor; the account unifies cases that previously were put in distinct categories under the single rubric of 'a cognitive shift enjoyed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: No serious practical concern engaged
rubrics_metrics.description: No serious practical concern is engaged (otherwise the shift triggers planning, fear, etc., not amusement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the situation demands immediate practical action (danger, urgent problem-solving), the cognitive shift will be subordinated to action and is unlikely to be experienced as humorous; consider context and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No strong negative emotion about the new state
rubrics_metrics.description: No strong negative emotion arises about the new state (otherwise the shift triggers grief, anger, disgust).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the shift is recognized, strong negative affect toward the new interpretation prevents the pleasure-in-shift required for humor; distinguish between negative-content humor (gallows humor within a play frame) and genuinely aversive emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience is in a play frame
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience is in a play frame that allows enjoying the shift itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'play frame' is a contextual stance permitting detached enjoyment of cognitive moves; whether an audience is in that frame depends on social cues, norms, and framing of the situation. Without the play frame, similar shifts can produce other reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift is non-trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift is non-trivial — the new state must genuinely differ from the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere restatement or negligible reinterpretation won't produce humor; the representational change must be substantial enough to register as a distinct cognitive state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three theoretical points any account must satisfy
rubrics_metrics.description: Morreall's three demands: (1) cognitive content — there is something the audience represents; (2) shift — that representation suddenly changes; (3) hedonic positive valence — the change is enjoyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A putative theory of humor that fails to include any one of these elements does not adequately capture what it is to have a humor experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for identifying humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a definite mental representation in play before the comic moment? Does that representation undergo a sudden change? Is the change enjoyed rather than mourned/feared? Has the audience been kept out of serious practical engagement? Could the same shift, in another context, produce horror, sadness, or wonder instead?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these questions to concrete cases to determine whether an experience qualifies as humor under the cognitive-shift account; use them to distinguish humor from surprise, horror, or amazement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical adequacy: must explain non-superiority cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful theory should account for laughter in cases where superiority does not apply (e.g., clever wordplay, laughing at oneself, or laughter at something judged better-than-expected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morreall criticizes superiority accounts as too narrow; evaluators should check whether a theory can explain self-directed humor, appreciation of virtuosity, and non-derogatory comic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical plausibility of physiological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory claims about physiology or 'release' mechanisms must be empirically plausible (e.g., hydraulic nervous-energy models are not supported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief models that rely on outdated physiological metaphors (hydraulic models of nervous energy) are suspect; assess empirical support for any physiological mechanism invoked to explain humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity accounts must add hedonic/play-frame conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure incongruity is too broad — incongruity-alone occurs in horror, surprise, and mystery; to yield humor an incongruity account must specify enjoyment and play-frame conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing an incongruity-based theory, require additional conditions that pick out when incongruity produces amusement rather than other reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolutionary/adaptive function: humor fosters mental flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor's pleasure in detecting and reframing mismatches encourages mental flexibility; this adaptive function situates the cognitive-shift account in an evolutionary-cognitive framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists can use evolutionary considerations to motivate why pleasure would be associated with cognitive shifts (reinforcing the habit of reframing), but empirical support and careful argumentation are needed to motivate adaptive claims.
